arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: the side that brought the case's counsel argued the statute relies on outdated assumptions about parental roles.
The government's counsel argued Congress must consider many factors when deciding who becomes a citizen.
Justices questioned whether the distinction between fathers and mothers is based on biology or stereotype.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests a statute that requires fathers to take extra steps to pass citizenship to children born outside the U.S. the side that brought the case argues this rule violates equal protection. The government argues the rule reflects biological realities and congressional judgment.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on November 10, 2010.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to strike down the citizenship statute as unconstitutional.
The government wants the Court to uphold the statute as a valid exercise of congressional power.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues the statute relies on gender stereotypes rather than legitimate biological differences.
The government argues the statute reflects Congress's broad authority to define who becomes a national.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Kennedy asked if the side that brought the case wants the Court to say Congress gets less deference on nationality than on admission.
Justice Scalia asked what separates a stereotype from a reality regarding parental care of illegitimate children.

paragraphs: The outcome defines the scope of congressional power over citizenship. It determines how the government treats parents of children born abroad. It shapes the legal standard for gender-based distinctions in nationality laws.
